title: The Angle-Defect Condition Is Necessary but Not Sufficient for Archimedean Solids
description: A rigorous answer to the open question raised by the Archimedean classification (platonic-solids-oq-02): can the angle constraint alone determine the 13 Archimedean types? The answer is no. Positive angle defect is a genuine necessary condition with real force - it caps vertex degree at five - but infinitely many vertex types (the family [3,3,n]) satisfy it while being neither Platonic nor among the 13 Archimedean solids. The missing ingredient is global geometric realizability, which a single-vertex angle sum cannot detect. Everything is proved over the rationals with norm_num / nlinarith / induction, with no native_decide, so it is genuinely axiom-free.

overview.historicalContext: The Archimedean solids — 13 convex polyhedra whose faces are regular polygons of two or more kinds arranged identically around every vertex — were catalogued by Archimedes (the work is lost, but Pappus attributes the list to him) and rediscovered during the Renaissance, with Kepler giving a complete treatment in *Harmonices Mundi* (1619). Their classification famously combines a *local* angular condition with a *global* geometric one. The local condition is positive angle defect: by Descartes' theorem on the total angular defect of a convex polyhedron (a discrete precursor of Gauss–Bonnet, the defects summing to $4\pi$), the regular polygons meeting at each vertex must leave an angular gap, i.e. their interior angles sum to strictly less than $2\pi$. The parent gallery entry verifies all 13 Archimedean vertex types satisfy this — but with `native_decide` (which invokes the `Lean.ofReduceBool` axiom) and with the classification itself left as a `True`-stub. It poses the natural question: is the angle condition, by itself, enough to single out the 13? This file settles that question over ℚ, axiom-free.
overview.problemStatement: Model a vertex by the list of its face sizes; a regular $n$-gon has interior angle $1 - 2/n$ in units of $\pi$, and the vertex has *positive defect* when $\sum_i (1 - 2/n_i) < 2$. The question (the parent's open question OQ-02-OQ-01): does positive angle defect alone determine the 13 Archimedean vertex types? The answer proved here is **no**. Positive defect is genuinely *necessary* — it forces the vertex degree $\le 5$ (`degree_le_five`) and all 13 types satisfy it — but it is decisively *not sufficient*: the family $[3,3,k+4]$ gives infinitely many vertex types that pass the test yet are neither Platonic (uniform) nor among the 13 Archimedean types.
overview.proofStrategy: Two halves. NECESSARY: every regular polygon's interior angle is at least a triangle's, $1/3$ (`angleFrac_ge_third`, by monotonicity of $1 - 2/n$); summing, a degree-$d$ vertex has angle sum $\ge d/3$, so positive defect forces $d/3 < 2$, i.e. $d \le 5$ (`degree_le_five`) — six equilateral triangles already tile the plane flatly with angle sum exactly $2$. SUFFICIENT-FAILURE: exhibit `family k = [3,3,k+4]`. Each has angle sum $5/3 - 2/(k+4) < 2$ (`family_positiveDefect`, via `nlinarith`); the map is injective in $k$ (`family_injective`); no member is uniform ($k+4 \ne 3$) or Archimedean (each length-3 Archimedean type has a second face $\ge 6$, the family's is a triangle). Packaging via `Set.infinite_of_injective_forall_mem` yields `infinitely_many_positiveDefect` and the sharp `infinitely_many_nonArchimedean_positiveDefect`. All 13 Archimedean checks are re-proved with `norm_num` over ℚ, eliminating the parent's `native_decide`.
keyInsights: The result is a clean *necessary-but-not-sufficient* separation: positive angle defect carries real combinatorial force (it bounds vertex degree at 5) yet is blind to the global constraint that actually picks out the 13 — convex geometric realizability. A purely local, single-vertex angular criterion provably cannot do the classification's work.

The degree bound is sharp and has a vivid meaning: $d/3 < 2 \iff d \le 5$ because six equilateral triangles meet with angle sum exactly $2$ (a flat tiling, zero defect). The triangle being the angle-minimizing polygon ($1/3 \le 1 - 2/n$) is exactly what makes 5 the ceiling.

The witnessing family $[3,3,k+4]$ is the simplest possible counterexample generator: fixing two triangles and growing the third face keeps the angle sum below $5/3 < 2$ forever, so an infinite, injective, non-Archimedean, non-uniform family passes — a finite set like the 13 can never be the exact solution set of such a condition.

The enrichment over the parent is also foundational: re-deriving the 13 angle-defect checks with `norm_num` over ℚ instead of `native_decide` removes the `Lean.ofReduceBool` dependency, so the supporting computations are genuinely axiom-free (only propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound) — a real upgrade in trust, not just style.

Modeling angles in units of $\pi$ over the rationals ($1 - 2/n \in \mathbb Q$) keeps the whole argument exact and `norm_num`-decidable, sidestepping any real-analysis or transcendence concerns while losing nothing — the comparison to $2$ is purely rational.

conclusion.summary: Positive angle defect is necessary but decisively not sufficient for the Archimedean classification. Necessary: it bounds the vertex degree at 5 (`degree_le_five`, since each regular polygon contributes at least a triangle's $1/3$ and $6 \cdot 1/3 = 2$ is already flat) and all 13 Archimedean vertex types satisfy it (`all_archimedean_positiveDefect`). Not sufficient: the injective family $[3,3,k+4]$ supplies infinitely many vertex types with positive defect that are neither uniform nor Archimedean (`infinitely_many_nonArchimedean_positiveDefect`), with $[3,3,4]$ and $[3,3,5]$ as smallest concrete witnesses. Everything is over ℚ via `norm_num`/`nlinarith`/`induction` — no `native_decide` — so it is genuinely axiom-free (only propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound).
conclusion.implications: The angle constraint alone cannot determine the 13 Archimedean solids: the decisive missing ingredient is the global geometric realizability (convex closure) that a single-vertex angle sum cannot detect. This sharply delimits how far the purely local/combinatorial approach the parent hoped for can go, and re-proving the supporting computations without `native_decide` upgrades the parent's angle-defect checks from `Lean.ofReduceBool`-dependent to genuinely axiom-free — a foundational improvement, not merely cosmetic.
openQuestions: Which *additional* local or semi-local condition, layered on top of positive angle defect, would cut the infinite positive-defect set down to exactly the 13 — e.g. requiring a globally consistent edge/face count (an Euler-characteristic constraint) or 2-uniformity across adjacent vertices?

Can one formalize Descartes' total-defect theorem ($\sum \text{defects} = 4\pi$ for a convex polyhedron) and use it to turn the per-vertex defect into the genuine global obstruction, recovering Kepler's completeness proof of the 13?
Does an analogous necessary-but-not-sufficient separation hold for the convex uniform tilings of the plane (the 11 Archimedean tilings), where the defect is exactly zero rather than positive?

originalContributions: Rational (norm_num-based) re-proof that all 13 Archimedean vertex types have positive angle defect, removing the parent's native_decide / Lean.ofReduceBool dependence
degree_le_five: at most five regular polygons meet at a vertex with positive angle defect (necessary direction with real combinatorial force)
angleFrac_ge_third: the interior angle of any regular n-gon (n>=3) is at least 1/3 of pi, the key monotonicity fact
family_positiveDefect: the infinite family [3,3,n] all have positive angle defect (angle sum 5/3 - 2/n)
infinitely_many_positiveDefect: the positive-defect condition admits infinitely many vertex types
infinitely_many_nonArchimedean_positiveDefect: infinitely many positive-defect types remain even after excluding Platonic and the 13 Archimedean types - the sharp answer to the open question (NO)
concrete_witnesses: the two smallest explicit counterexamples [3,3,4] and [3,3,5]
meta.assumptions: 0 axioms, 0 sorries. Every theorem depends only on the standard foundational axioms propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound (verified via #print axioms); in particular there is no Lean.ofReduceBool (no native_decide) and no sorryAx. The angle model is the standard one: a regular n-gon has interior angle (n-2)/n in units of pi; positive defect means the angles at a vertex sum to strictly less than 2.

sections.title: Module Overview and the Angle Model
sections.summary: Docstring stating the open question and the answer, then the rational angle model: angleFrac (interior angle in units of pi), vertexAngleSum, and PositiveDefect.
sections.mathContext: A regular n-gon has interior angle (n-2)/n = 1 - 2/n in units of pi. A vertex has positive angle defect when the faces meeting there leave an angular gap, i.e. the angle sum is < 2.

sections.title: Triangle Is the Sharpest: angleFrac >= 1/3
sections.summary: angleFrac_ge_third: the interior angle of any regular polygon with at least three sides is at least 1/3 of pi (attained by the equilateral triangle).
sections.mathContext: Since 1 - 2/n is increasing in n, its minimum over n >= 3 is 1 - 2/3 = 1/3. This is the key bound driving the degree cap.

sections.title: Necessary Direction: At Most Five Faces per Vertex
sections.summary: A generic list lower bound (list_sum_lb), the angle-sum bound vertexAngleSum_ge (>= degree * 1/3), and degree_le_five: positive defect forces at most five faces at a vertex.
sections.mathContext: If each of d faces contributes at least 1/3 and the total is < 2, then d/3 < 2, so d <= 5. Six equilateral triangles give angle sum exactly 2 (a flat tiling), the boundary case.

sections.title: All 13 Archimedean Types Pass (axiom-free)
sections.summary: archimedeanTypes lists the 13 vertex types; all_archimedean_positiveDefect re-proves each has positive defect via norm_num over the rationals, replacing the parent's native_decide.
sections.mathContext: This confirms positive defect is genuinely necessary for the 13, while removing the Lean.ofReduceBool dependence of the parent's computational checks.

sections.title: Insufficiency: An Infinite Family Passes
sections.summary: The witness family [3,3,n], its positive defect (family_positiveDefect), injectivity, absence from the 13 (family_not_archimedean), and non-uniformity (family_not_uniform).
sections.mathContext: [3,3,n] has angle sum 1/3 + 1/3 + (1 - 2/n) = 5/3 - 2/n < 2 for every n >= 3. For n >= 4 it is non-uniform and not one of the 13, since no length-3 Archimedean type has the shape [3,3,*].

sections.title: The Answer: Infinitely Many Non-Archimedean Witnesses
sections.summary: infinitely_many_positiveDefect and infinitely_many_nonArchimedean_positiveDefect establish that the angle condition admits infinitely many vertex types even after excluding Platonic and Archimedean ones; concrete_witnesses gives [3,3,4] and [3,3,5].
sections.mathContext: Since a finite list can never equal an infinite set, no single-vertex angle/combinatorial criterion can determine the 13 Archimedean solids; global geometric realizability is the decisive missing ingredient.
